chunks: "Program memory stores the instructions the CPU executes. Data memory stores the values those instructions work on: variables, buffers, the stack.
At the highest level they're distinguished by how the CPU uses them.
The program counter walks through program memory, mostly in order, and it's essentially read-only while the program runs.
Data memory is accessed by load and store instructions at whatever addresses the program computes, and it's constantly read and written.
In a Harvard architecture, like an AVR or PIC microcontroller, those are two physically separate memories with separate buses and sometimes separate address spaces.
For example, an ATmega328P has 32 KB of flash for program and 2 KB of SRAM for data.
The advantage is that you can fetch the next instruction while the current one is accessing data, so you don't have a bus bottleneck.
In a von Neumann architecture, both live in one memory and share a bus, so you have more flexibility, you can treat code as data and load programs dynamically, but fetch and data access compete.
Most modern CPUs split the difference. The L1 instruction and data caches are separate, but below that it's one shared main memory."
